analysis.one_liner: Repeals the estate tax rule that taxes wealth-freezing transfers to heirs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one hearing on May 17, 1989 and just 2 cosponsors, it died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike a 1988 estate tax rule (section 2036(c)) that was written to stop a technique called a "freeze." In a freeze, a business owner keeps the fixed-value stock while giving the growth stock to heirs, so all future growth in the business escapes estate tax. Repealing the rule — retroactively to transfers made after December 17, 1987 — would once again let large estate values escape taxation on everything the business earns after the transfer.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of valuable family businesses and other very wealthy families who could use freeze techniques would pass future business growth to heirs free of estate tax. Because the repeal would apply back to transfers after December 17, 1987, families who had already used freezes in that window would get a retroactive tax saving. Estate planning professionals would gain a market for the newly unpenalized freeze arrangements.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 2036(c) of the tax code, the rule added in 1988 that pulls the later growth of a business back into a deceased owner's taxable estate when the owner kept an interest and transferred shares to family members.
Applies the repeal retroactively to property transferred after December 17, 1987, wiping out the new rule's effect on freezes already in place.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less estate tax from very large estates, because the value a business gains after a freeze transfer would no longer be taxed when the original owner dies. That lost revenue either has to be made up by other taxpayers or added to deficits. The estate tax is paid almost entirely by multimillion-dollar estates, so the benefit is concentrated at the top while the cost is spread across everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers via lost estate revenue

drawbacks.text: The repeal would reopen a major loophole: an owner could lock in today's estate value and hand decades of future business growth to heirs untouched by estate tax, shrinking a tax only the largest estates ever pay.
Making the repeal retroactive to December 17, 1987 would reward families that had already rushed to set up freezes after the rule was signed, a benefit unavailable to estates that had not.

The good-faith case for repeal was that section 2036(c) was blunt: it swept in ordinary succession planning where a parent keeps an income interest, and it created uncertainty for families trying to hand a business to the next generation. Congress had passed it only months earlier, and critics said it went too far.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The legitimate complaint — that the 1988 anti-freeze rule was broad and complicated — is real, but the fix in this bill was the opposite of a narrow one: it would delete the rule outright and apply that deletion retroactively, letting wealthy families shelter unlimited future business growth from estate tax. The savings would go to a small number of the largest estates while the revenue burden shifted to everyone else. A tighter repair of the rule would have been a far better-balanced answer.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and heard once, but the committee never voted to send it to the floor and the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: Senator Howell Heflin introduced the bill on April 19, 1989; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
The bill picked up only 2 cosponsors, one Democrat and one Republican, over its lifetime.
The Finance Committee held a hearing on May 17, 1989 — the only action the bill ever received beyond introduction and referral.
No markup, no floor vote, and no House action ever followed; the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax's anti-freeze rule stayed on the books, so the federal estate tax continued to capture business growth shifted out of large estates. The families and estate planners who wanted the retroactive break got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The estate tax base and general taxpayers

for.name: Sen. Howell Heflin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 19, 1989 to repeal the estate tax freeze rule retroactively.

for.name: One Senate Democrat and one Senate Republican
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on May 17, 1989 but never voted to report the bill to the Senate floor, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a recorded vote; sponsorship was bipartisan but tiny, with a Democratic sponsor and one cosponsor from each party.

industries.industry: Wealthy family business owners and large estates
industries.note: The bill's entire purpose was to relieve these estates: repealing section 2036(c) would let an owner freeze the taxable value of a business while heirs take all future growth tax-free, retroactive to transfers after December 17, 1987. The public's cost is the estate tax revenue and progressivity that would disappear with it.

With the anti-freeze rule repealed, lawyers and planners would once again be able to sell freeze arrangements to wealthy clients without the tax penalty Congress imposed in 1988. Their gain is paid for in foregone estate tax on the very estates they serve.
